summary: This document defines a parameter for SVCB and HTTPS DNS records to say a service is reachable using Oblivious HTTP, through an Oblivious Gateway Resource. It also defines how to learn the key configuration of that gateway.

plainLanguage.summary: A sign on a shop says "you can order here through a blind mail slot," and tells you how to seal your note to it.

questions: how to discover an oblivious http gateway
subtitle: A DNS parameter that tells clients a service can be reached with Oblivious HTTP, and where to find its keys.

tldr.problem: Oblivious HTTP deployments usually share gateway and key information in bespoke ways, which makes it hard for clients to discover services that support it.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9540 defines an empty ohttp parameter for SVCB and HTTPS DNS records, a well-known URI /.well-known/ohttp-gateway for the gateway, and a GET with the application/ohttp-keys media type to fetch the gateway's key configuration.
tldr.outcome: Clients can learn dynamically that a target has an Oblivious HTTP gateway and fetch its keys, though they must guard against key and dohpath targeting attacks.

today: RFC 9540 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2024, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on Oblivious HTTP in RFC 9458 and the SVCB records in RFC 9460.

sections.title: Why Oblivious Services Need Discovery
sections.content:
Oblivious HTTP (RFC 9458) lets a client encrypt messages to an Oblivious Target Resource. The messages are wrapped in encrypted messages sent to an Oblivious Gateway Resource, reached through an Oblivious Relay Resource that proxies them and hides the client's identity. The relay cannot read the messages, and the gateway and target cannot learn the client's identity from a single transaction.

Deployments are often coordinated by hand, so key configuration is shared in a bespoke fashion. Some deployments want more dynamic discovery. For example, a network might run a DNS resolver that is reachable using Oblivious HTTP and want to advertise it using DDR (RFC 9462) or DNR (RFC 9463).

This RFC does not help discover relays. Relay configuration is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Some shops let you send orders through a go-between so the shop never learns who you are. This document is about how you find out which shops do that.

sections.title: Where the Mechanism Applies
sections.content:
The RFC names two models. In the first, a client wants to talk to a specific target service and prefers Oblivious HTTP when it is offered, so it upgrades from non-proxied HTTP once it learns about the gateway. In the second, a client has a default target, such as a public DNS resolver reachable over Oblivious HTTP, and is willing to use discovered alternatives that may give more optimized or more relevant responses.

In both models the client is configured with a relay it trusts. That relay needs to offer either generic access to gateways or a service that lets clients check which gateways are accessible.
sections.plainLanguage: You either switch to the private mail slot at a shop you already use, or you try other shops that offer one. Either way you use a mail carrier you already trust.

sections.title: The ohttp SvcParamKey
sections.content:
The ohttp parameter in a Service Binding (SVCB) record (RFC 9460) says that the service can be used as a target through an associated gateway. Both its presentation and wire-format values MUST be empty.

A service that is only reachable through Oblivious HTTP can list ohttp in the mandatory list, which makes clients that do not understand the parameter ignore that record. Without mandatory, the record advertises optional availability. Several records can describe separate configurations.

For the https scheme, the parameter means the target is an Oblivious HTTP service using the default message/bhttp media type. For the dns scheme (RFC 9461), it means the DNS server has a DNS-over-HTTPS service (RFC 8484) reachable with Oblivious HTTP. Inner requests use the application/dns-message media type, and the alpn parameter MUST include at least one HTTP value such as h2 or h3. Other schemes that want to use the parameter MUST define its meaning.

Only publicly accessible DoH resolvers will generally work as Oblivious HTTP targets, unless a relay is deployed in coordination to reach network-specific resolvers.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a tiny flag on the shop's address card that says "mail slot available." If the flag is marked required, shops that do not know the flag skip the card.

sections.title: Discovery With DDR and DNR
sections.content:
With DDR, a client can find that a DoH resolver supports Oblivious HTTP by querying _dns.resolver.arpa or by using a resolver's name. The client must still do the TLS certificate checks from DDR. Since gateway and target need to be on the same host, the client checks the certificate the gateway presents, which can happen while fetching the key configuration, directly or through the relay or another proxy so that its IP address is not exposed.

Opportunistic Discovery, which validates only the IP address, SHOULD NOT generally be used with Oblivious HTTP. If it must be used, the client MUST ensure the relay only accesses the gateway and target using the resolver's original unencrypted IP address.

The parameter can also be used with DNR, where the oblivious configuration and path parameters can travel in DHCP and Router Advertisement messages. In both cases clients must ensure they are not targeted with unique DoH paths that would reveal their identity.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network tells you about its helpers, you still check their ID. And you make sure nobody hands you a special, one-of-a-kind address that could identify you.

sections.title: Finding the Gateway and Its Keys
sections.content:
The RFC defines a well-known resource, /.well-known/ohttp-gateway, which is an Oblivious Gateway Resource on the same host as the Target Resource. A server that does not want to run the gateway there can use 3xx redirects, which apply both to key configuration requests and to encapsulated requests made through a relay.

If a client is redirected while fetching the keys, it MUST NOT tell the relay the redirected URI as the gateway location, since the gateway could encode client-identifying values in it. Relays used with dynamically discovered gateways MUST use the well-known resource and follow redirects on their own. They can remember redirects across requests.

To get the key configuration, the client sends a GET to the gateway URI, directly or through a proxy, with Accept: application/ohttp-keys. Gateways that coordinate with targets advertising Oblivious HTTP SHOULD support this, unless another out-of-band configuration model is available. The reply carries the key configuration in the body with content type application/ohttp-keys. Fetching directly exposes the client's IP address to the gateway, so a proxy can be used to hide it.
sections.plainLanguage: Every shop with a mail slot puts it in the same predictable place. You ask for the slot's lock details first, ideally through a helper, so the shop does not see you.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Attackers can strip SVCB information from cleartext DNS answers not protected by DNSSEC, which can downgrade clients. Because the indication is only a hint, a client can always check the well-known gateway location for a key configuration. Encrypted DNS with DNSSEC also helps.

Fetching a key configuration without a proxy can expose the client's IP address. In key targeting attacks, a gateway hands unique key configurations to specific clients so their requests can be linked. Clients SHOULD use some mitigation, such as confirming the key with a shared proxy. If a client detects per-client keys, it can stop using the gateway and possibly report the attack.

The same idea applies to dohpath: an attacker could use unique values to identify clients. A client can avoid this by allowing only a single dohpath value such as /dns-query{?dns}, or else SHOULD run a consistency check, perhaps on only a percentage of discovery events.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky shop might give each customer a slightly different lock so it can tell them apart. Customers protect themselves by comparing locks with others.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC adds an entry to the "Service Parameter Keys (SvcParamKeys)" registry: number 8, name ohttp, meaning that a service operates an Oblivious HTTP target, with the IETF as change controller. It also adds the well-known URI suffix ohttp-gateway to the "Well-Known URIs" registry, with status permanent.
sections.plainLanguage: The flag and the shop's standard mail-slot spot are written in the official lists so everyone agrees on them.

data.title: HTTPS records with ohttp
data.code:
svc.example.com. 7200  IN HTTPS 1 . ( alpn=h2 ohttp )

svc.example.com. 7200  IN HTTPS 1 . ( mandatory=ohttp ohttp )

data.title: Fetching the gateway key configuration
data.code:
GET /.well-known/ohttp-gateway HTTP/1.1
Host: svc.example.com
Accept: application/ohttp-keys
